title: Boundary-accessible work in a collision-charged topological quantum battery
authors: Osman Orçun Keskin, Özgür E. Müstecaplıoğlu
abstract: Quantum batteries store energy in nonequilibrium quantum states. The ergotropy sets the work extractable by an arbitrary global unitary, but a device usually exchanges energy through a single local port. It remains unclear how much stored work such a port can deliver, and whether topological edge modes help. We study a dimerized spin chain of Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) type. Excited two-level ancillas charge it at one end by repeated collisions, and an initially empty two-level load discharges it at the same site. An exact free-fermion mapping yields a bound on the load work for all number-conserving quadratic extraction protocols. The load gains extractable work only if a single-particle mode of the battery holds more than half an excitation. Resonant charging fills the topological edge mode above this threshold. A single boundary pulse then delivers 98.6% of the maximal load work allowed by the bound for representative parameters. Under the same six-collision controls, the trivial-phase load remains passive. Within the protocol that selects the load pulse for maximum delivered work, cycle power peaks at a finite collision number while delivered work continues to increase over the scanned range. Over the tested range, the advantage survives hopping disorder, which preserves chiral symmetry. On-site disorder breaks this symmetry and leaves a finite fraction of loads passive. Topology thus supplies a localized access channel, while spectral matching and symmetry decide whether stored energy becomes usable local work.
summary: This paper analyzes work extraction from a topological quantum battery modeled by an SSH chain. It demonstrates that the ability to extract work locally is dictated not by the total stored energy, but by the occupation of the topological edge mode. A single boundary pulse can efficiently access nearly the maximum possible work, highlighting topology's role in creating usable local energy channels.
main_problem: The study investigates how much stored work in a quantum battery, modeled by a topological spin chain, can be accessed through a single local port, and whether topological edge modes enhance this accessibility.
main_result: The load can only access stored work if a single-particle mode holds more than half an excitation, and a single boundary pulse can deliver 98.6% of the theoretically maximal load work allowed by the bound.
method: The analysis employs free-fermion mapping to derive bounds on extractable work (ergotropy) and simulates charging/discharging protocols using the SSH model Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The system is a hard-core Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) chain acting as a quantum battery, coupled to a two-level charger and a load. The dynamics are analyzed using quadratic Hamiltonians and correlation matrix evolution.
key_observables:
Load work ($W_L$), cycle efficiency ($\eta_{	ext{cyc}}$), boundary occupation ($
u_{	ext{edge}}$), and global ergotropy ($W$).
important_parameters:
The critical threshold for load activation is $
u_{\max} > 1/2$; the advantage is tested against hopping and on-site disorder.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to number-conserving quadratic extraction protocols, and some results rely on approximations for edge mode splitting.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the SSH battery structure, the charging/discharging protocol, and comparative diagnostics showing topological vs. trivial phase behavior regarding boundary occupation and work extraction.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model and the work bound, then analyzes the charging dynamics, demonstrating that topological edge modes provide a localized, highly efficient access channel for extracting work, even when global ergotropy suggests otherwise.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the fundamental question of energy transduction in quantum systems, showing how topological protection can localize and enhance usable energy extraction at interfaces, which is crucial for quantum energy storage devices.
